findings.title: [P1] Fix inverted non-finite check letting NaN/Infinity bypass validation
findings.body: Trigger: any input `Number()` cannot parse finitely — e.g. `"abc"`, `"5s"`, `"Infinity"`, `"1e999"`. `Number("abc")` is `NaN`, `Number.isFinite(NaN)` is `false`, so the `&&` at `src/options.ts:11` short-circuits and the `throw` is skipped; the function returns `NaN` (or `±Infinity`). The old code threw `"invalid timeout"` for all of these (`Number.parseInt` yields `NaN`, failing `!Number.isSafeInteger`). A validator silently returning an unusable number breaks the error contract under realistic invalid input — downstream, `setTimeout(fn, NaN)` behaves as a 0ms timer, masking the failure. The guard should reject non-finite values, e.g. `if (!Number.isFinite(timeout) || !Number.isSafeInteger(timeout) || timeout <= 0) throw ...`.

findings.title: [P2] Restore base-10 integer parsing grammar for timeout strings
findings.body: Replacing `Number.parseInt(value, 10)` with `Number(value)` at `src/options.ts:10` changes observable parsing semantics beyond the validation refinement: `"0x10"` previously threw (parsed as `0`, failing `timeout <= 0`) but now returns `16`; `"1e3"` previously returned `1` but now silently returns `1000`; `"1.9"` previously returned `1` but now throws. Each contradicts the PR's stated goal of "preserving existing contracts" for a value that callers treat as a millisecond timeout. Keeping `Number.parseInt(value, 10)` (with the corrected non-finite guard) preserves the prior grammar.
